transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, yeah, thanks for fitting me in. So, as for what brings me in... well, it’s been building up for a while, honestly. I’d say for the past year or so, I’ve just been having this issue where every little thing completely derails me. And I mean the absolute smallest things. 

Like, I’ll be in my office—I run my own company, built it from the ground up since I didn't exactly finish high school, so I’m used to juggling a lot of moving parts—but lately, if my phone just gives a tiny buzz on the desk, not even a ring, just a vibration, I’m completely pulled away from my work. Or if somebody just walks past my office door. I had these glass walls put in a few years ago because I thought it was a great idea for company culture, you know, transparency and all that, but now it’s like every time an employee even walks by to get coffee, my brain just snaps right to them. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around me in the room. It’s in my own head, too. I’ll be right in the middle of looking at quarterly numbers or something important, and suddenly I have a totally random thought about my in-laws—like, wondering what my father-in-law is going to say about the upcoming holidays, or if they're visiting—and boom, it pulls me completely off what I’m doing before I can even stop it. I catch myself ten minutes later realizing I'm not even looking at my screen anymore. It's just been happening constantly for the last year, and it's driving me a little crazy.
Do you feel anxious when you get pulled away from your work by these distractions?

Well, anxious? I wouldn’t really say anxious. It’s not like my heart is pounding or I’m sitting there worrying that the company is going to go under because I looked away for a second. It’s more... well, let me explain it like this. When that phone buzzes, or when I start thinking about my father-in-law, I don’t feel a sense of dread or panic or anything like that. I just feel this sudden, almost automatic urge to go follow that new thought. 

Like, if I’m looking at the quarterly reports and an employee walks by the glass, I don’t feel nervous about them seeing me or anything, I just suddenly have to know where they’re going. Are they going to the breakroom? Did we get that new espresso machine installed yet? Because I actually spent like three hours researching commercial espresso machines last month—I wanted the team to have really good coffee, you know, to boost morale, since I'm big on company culture—and then suddenly I’m looking up local coffee bean roasters on my computer instead of doing the financials. 

So, no, anxiety definitely isn't the right word for it. It’s more like... frustration, but only after the fact. Like, I’ll realize ten or twenty minutes later that I haven’t done any of the actual work I was supposed to be doing, and I’ll be annoyed with myself. But in the exact moment when I’m actually getting pulled away? There’s no anxiety at all. I just completely forget what I was doing and happily go down whatever rabbit hole just opened up. My wife always asks if I’m stressed or anxious at work because I end up having to stay late to catch up, but it’s really not stress. It’s just that I lost half my afternoon chasing every little thought that popped into my head, you know? So yeah, definitely not anxious.
Do you find yourself repeating certain actions or rituals throughout the day?

Rituals? Like... doing things over and over in a specific way? No, no, definitely not. I mean, honestly, I'm probably the exact opposite of that. I can't even stick to a basic morning routine, let alone some kind of strict ritual. 

My wife—she’s a dental hygienist, very organized, very methodical—she has this whole routine where she gets up, drinks exactly eight ounces of water, does ten minutes of yoga, makes the bed, and has her coffee. Every single day. I watch her do it and I just think, how on earth do you do the exact same thing every morning without losing your mind? Because for me, every day is completely different. Sometimes I’ll get up and immediately start pacing around the kitchen while checking my emails on my phone, and I won't even realize I haven't made coffee until an hour later. Other times I’ll jump right into the shower, but then I'll remember I needed to put the trash out, so I'll hop out, dripping wet, to grab the bins. 

So yeah, no repeating actions or anything like that. I don't have to tap the desk three times before I sit down or anything. Honestly, it's kind of a running joke at the office that nobody ever knows how I'm going to start a meeting. Am I going to start with a joke? Am I going to dive right into the numbers? Am I going to spend five minutes talking about a documentary I watched the night before about deep-sea welding? It’s a total toss-up. So no, no rituals or anything like that. I just kind of fly by the seat of my pants, which, you know, has worked out okay for the business, but it definitely means I don't have any repetitive habits. If anything, I could probably use a little more routine, but my brain just doesn't seem to want to operate that way.
Do you often find it hard to finish tasks because you get distracted or lose interest?

Well, yeah, absolutely. That’s—that’s actually a huge part of the problem. Finishing things is... it’s tough. Starting things? I’m great at starting things. I have a million ideas, which is why I started the company in the first place, but seeing them through to the end is where I just hit a wall. 

Like, I can sit down to write up a new planning document, right? Or I’ll sit down with one of my managers for a one-on-one, and for the first few minutes, I am completely locked in. I’m engaged, I’m fired up, I’m ready to tackle whatever the issue is. But then... it’s like my brain just decides it’s had enough of that particular topic. Pretty soon, I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the manager’s tie—wondering where he bought it, if it’s silk, if I should start wearing ties again even though we have a casual dress code—and suddenly I realize I missed half of what he just said. I have to stop him and say, "Hey, sorry, can you run that back for me?" And it’s embarrassing, you know? I’m the CEO, I should be able to listen to my own managers. 

Or with the planning documents, I’ll get the header done, write the first paragraph, and then I’m just... gone. I lose interest completely, and I end up opening twelve other tabs on my browser to look at completely unrelated things. I’ve got half-finished documents and spreadsheets all over my desktop. It’s like my brain just runs out of gas for whatever I’m supposed to be doing, and I have to go find something new and shiny to look at. So yeah, finishing tasks is a real struggle. It’s just so hard to keep that initial momentum going once the novelty wears off, you know?
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Act on impulse without thinking about the consequences? Um... no, I wouldn't say that. I really don't think I do that. I mean, sure, I move fast. You have to move fast in business. But I wouldn't call it acting without thinking about what's going to happen next. Actually, it's kind of the opposite, because when you're the guy in charge, everything falls on your shoulders, right? I mean, I didn't even finish high school, so I don't have some fancy MBA or safety net to fall back on. Everything I built, I built by trusting my gut, but my gut is always calculating the risks. 

Like, people might see me make a quick call and think, "Oh, he's just being impulsive." For example, a couple of months ago, we had this supplier who kept missing delivery windows, and I just cut them off right in the middle of a phone call. Just said, "We're done, cancel the contract." My operations manager was absolutely freaking out, thinking I just ruined our supply chain on a whim. He was practically hyperventilating in my office, telling me I didn't think about the consequences. But I *did*. I already knew we had two backup vendors we could scale up, and I knew the late deliveries were costing us more in client goodwill than a temporary inventory dip would. I just processed all that in about ten seconds instead of calling a two-week committee meeting to debate it. 

So, no, I don't just do things recklessly. I might talk out of turn sometimes or jump into a project before the ink is completely dry on the proposal, but I always know what the stakes are. I'm not out here gambling the company payroll in Vegas or buying things we can't afford just for the thrill of it. I care way too much about my employees and the business to do something truly reckless like that. So, yeah, I definitely think things through... I just think them through a lot faster than other people expect me to, which I guess can look like an impulse to them, but to me, it's just being decisive. So no, I wouldn't say I ignore the consequences.
Do you have trouble organizing your time or tasks?

Organizing my time? Um, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble with that. I mean, I run a whole company, you know? You can't really do that if you don't know how to manage your time. I actually think I'm pretty good at it, all things considered. 

Like, I have a system. It might not look like a system to someone else, but it works for me. I use my calendar app for everything—meetings, calls, when I need to leave the office to pick up my dry cleaning, all of it. And I have my assistant, Sarah, who is an absolute lifesaver. She keeps me on track. If I'm supposed to be somewhere, she makes sure I know about it. She'll literally walk into my office and say, "Hey, you have that call with the marketing team in five minutes," and I'll drop whatever I'm doing and get on the call. 

So, it's not like I'm constantly missing deadlines or forgetting appointments. I mean, sure, my desk might look like a disaster area to someone else. There are papers everywhere, sticky notes stuck to the monitor, coffee cups I haven't taken back to the breakroom... but I know exactly where everything is. If you ask me for the Q3 projections, I know they're under the pile of mail on the left side of my desk, right next to the stapler. It's organized chaos, I guess you could call it. 

And as far as tasks go, I just tackle them as they come. I don't sit down and write out a meticulous to-do list every morning, color-coded by priority, because honestly, things change so fast in my line of work that a list like that would be obsolete by 10:00 AM anyway. I just prioritize on the fly. Whatever is the most urgent, whatever is on fire, that's what I deal with first. And if something falls through the cracks, well, that's just business. You can't catch everything. But overall, no, I don't feel like I struggle to organize my time or my tasks. I get things done, and the business is growing, so I must be doing something right, right? It's just a different way of operating.
Do you find it hard to focus on one thing for a long time?

Yeah, I mean, that really goes back to exactly what I was just telling you a few minutes ago. Focusing for a *long* time on just one single thing is... well, honestly, it's exhausting. It really is. 

Like I said before, I can start a planning document, or I'll sit down with one of my managers—take my VP of Sales, Mark, for example. Great guy, brilliant at his job, built our whole outbound strategy from scratch, but man, he loves to get into the granular details. So we'll sit down in my office, and for the first few minutes? I am completely locked in. I'm engaged, I'm tracking every metric he's giving me, we're going back and forth, and I'm totally in the zone. But if we stay on that exact same topic for too long... it's like a switch just flips in my head. 

I don't even mean to do it, it's not like I don't care about the sales numbers, but my brain just sort of unplugs and wanders off. I'll be sitting there looking right at him, nodding my head like I'm following along perfectly, and then I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I completely missed half of what was just said. I have no idea what he's been talking about for the last five minutes. It's incredibly frustrating, not to mention embarrassing, because then I have to stop him, swallow my pride, and say, "Hey, I'm really sorry, my mind went somewhere else—can you run that back for me?" And he has to start all over. 

And it's the exact same story with those planning documents I mentioned earlier. The first ten minutes, I'm a machine. I'm typing away, getting all the big ideas down. But asking me to sit there and focus on that one document for an hour or two without jumping to something else? It just doesn't happen. I have to break away, I have to open another tab, I have to check my email, because holding my attention on that one single track for a long stretch just feels almost physically impossible. It's like my brain just refuses to stay in one place for too long.
Do you have trouble controlling your emotions?

Controlling my emotions? Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, you can't exactly run a successful company if you're flying off the handle every time something goes wrong, right? People look to you for stability. Like, just last week, we had this massive issue with our payroll software. The whole system just completely crashed on a Thursday, and Friday is payday. Now, a lot of guys in my position—especially guys who built everything from the ground up without a fancy degree or a trust fund, like I was telling you earlier—they might completely lose it. They might start yelling at the IT guys, kicking the trash can, just totally panicking. 

But me? I didn't do any of that. I just took a deep breath, walked out to the main floor, and told everyone that there was a glitch but nobody was going home without getting paid. Just laid it out plain and simple so people wouldn't worry. And then I just methodically sat down and worked with the bank and the software vendor for the next six hours straight until we fixed it. So, sure, I feel the stress. I feel the pressure, absolutely. It is like this heavy weight on my chest sometimes, especially when people's livelihoods are on the line and it all comes back to me. But I don't let it control me. I don't explode at my staff or break down or anything like that. 

I mean, sure, I might get a little animated when I am excited about a new deal, or I might talk a little louder than I need to when I am trying to make a point in a crowded room, but that is just passion, you know? That is just me caring about the work. It is definitely not losing control. And honestly, if I could not control my emotions, my assistant Sarah would have quit years ago. She does not tolerate nonsense at all. But we work great together because I keep things level. Even when things go sideways, which they inevitably do because it is business and you can never predict everything, I just focus on the solution. I just pivot. So, no, emotional control is not really an issue for me. I keep it pretty well locked down, all things considered.
Do you often find yourself lacking motivation to start tasks?

Motivation? Wow, no. Honestly, if anything, it's the exact opposite for me. I mean, I am always ready to go. You don't get to where I am, running a whole operation, by sitting around waiting to feel inspired to do something, you know? Especially someone like me. I think I might have mentioned earlier, I didn't even finish high school. No diploma, no fancy college network to hand me a cushy job. When you're in that position, you absolutely cannot afford to lack motivation. You have to hustle every single day just to prove you belong in the room. So drive has never, ever been an issue for me. 

I'm the kind of guy who wakes up at 5 AM, usually before my alarm even goes off. My brain just clicks on, and I'm instantly thinking about what we're doing next, what deals we can close, how we can push the needle forward. Like, just yesterday morning, I was standing in the kitchen waiting for my coffee to brew, and this whole idea for restructuring our client onboarding process just hit me. I didn't stand there thinking, "Ugh, I really don't want to deal with this right now." I literally grabbed my laptop right there at the kitchen island and started mapping the whole thing out before the sun was even fully up. 

Actually, starting things is probably my favorite part of the job. I love the rush of a new project. Getting a new initiative off the ground, pitching a new client, kicking off a new marketing campaign... that's where I thrive. It's like, give me a blank slate and I'm all over it. I don't need anyone to push me or hype me up because I'm usually the one hyping everyone else up. If I lacked the motivation to start tasks, we wouldn't have launched those three new service tiers last year, and we definitely wouldn't be expanding into the new office space next month. I just dive right in. Sometimes I probably dive in a little too fast, honestly, before all the red tape is sorted out, but I just want to get moving. So, no, getting started is never the problem for me. I have more than enough motivation to go around.
Do you have trouble waiting for your turn or standing in line?

Waiting? No, not really. I mean, it's kind of funny you ask that, because I think a lot of people just assume that guys in my position—running a company, always moving, always onto the next big thing—would absolutely lose their minds if they had to just stand there and wait for something. But honestly, it doesn't bother me at all. I actually kind of... well, I don't want to say I enjoy it, but I definitely don't mind it. 

Take the airport, for example. I fly a lot for work, mostly domestic, visiting our regional hubs, pitching new clients, that sort of thing. And even with TSA PreCheck—which, let me tell you, is an absolute lifesaver if you travel as much as I do—sometimes you just hit a massive wall of people. Like, just last month, I was flying out of O'Hare on a Tuesday morning, and for whatever reason, the line was just wrapped all the way around the terminal. You look around, and there are all these guys in expensive suits huffing and puffing, checking their watches, tapping their feet, complaining to the staff. 

But me? I just see it as free time. It's rare downtime. I'll pull out my phone, I'll clear out my inbox, maybe shoot off a few quick texts to Sarah—my assistant, I mentioned her earlier, she's the one who keeps my life running—just to make sure the afternoon schedule is totally locked in. Or, if I don't feel like looking at a screen, I'll just stand there and run through the quarterly projections in my head. It's actually one of the few times during the day where nobody is actively knocking on my door demanding a decision right that second, you know? 

And it's the exact same thing with waiting my turn in a meeting or a conversation. If I'm listening to a vendor pitch or one of my department heads is giving a presentation, I can wait until they're completely finished to jump in. I mean, sure, I might have a dozen different thoughts and ideas firing off in my head all at once while they're talking, but I know how to hold off until it's actually my turn to speak. It's just basic professional respect, really. You can't run a successful boardroom if you're just talking over everyone the second a thought pops into your head. So yeah, waiting in line, waiting my turn... it's never really been an issue for me. I just use that time to get other things sorted out mentally.
Do you ever find yourself feeling overly emotional or reactive to situations, even if you don't act on those feelings?

Overly emotional on the inside? Um... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, I know some people use that metaphor, right? The whole swan thing—gliding smooth and calm on top of the water, but underneath they're just paddling like crazy and completely freaking out. But that's honestly not me. 

I really think my exterior matches my interior. When you're running a company, you can't even afford to *feel* reactive, you know? It's not just about hiding it from the staff so they don't panic; it's about actually keeping your own head clear so you can make the right call. Like, take last quarter, for example. We had this massive supplier issue. A huge shipment of raw materials got held up at customs, completely out of nowhere. Now, a lot of guys in my position would be sweating bullets, lying awake at night, their stomach in knots, just feeling that internal panic and rage even if they managed to put on a brave face at the office. 

But me? I honestly didn't feel that spike of emotion. I didn't feel this overwhelming urge to scream that I had to suppress. I just looked at the logistics report—it was a Tuesday, I remember because Sarah had just brought in the revised weekly schedule—and I just immediately thought, "Okay, what is the workaround?" I didn't feel angry at the customs agents, I didn't feel devastated about the project timelines. I just instantly shifted into problem-solving mode. 

Because if you let yourself feel all those extreme emotions, even just internally, it clouds your judgment. It eats up your mental bandwidth. And my bandwidth is already maxed out with a hundred different decisions a day. I mean, sure, if someone cuts me off in traffic or something, I might get a quick flash of annoyance, like literally anyone would, but it doesn't linger. It doesn't consume me. I don't sit there stewing in it or feeling like my blood is boiling while I'm smiling through a meeting. I just process whatever the situation is and move on to the next thing. I really think that's why I've been able to scale the business the way I have, because I don't get bogged down in all those heavy, reactive feelings that seem to paralyze other people. I just... I don't really operate that way, inside or out.
Do you find it hard to pay attention to details?

Details? No. No, definitely not. Actually, it's kind of the exact opposite for me. I mean, you can't run an operation doing the kind of volume we do if you're letting the little things slip through the cracks. A lot of people think that guys at the top, the executives, just sit around looking at the "big picture" all day and leave all the granular stuff to the lower-level guys. But honestly? That is exactly how you go broke. Especially when you started from the bottom like I did. When you don't have that formal education to fall back on, you learn real quick that the devil is absolutely in the details. 

Like, just to give you an example, last Thursday we were in the final stages of renegotiating a massive lease agreement for our new warehouse space—the one I mentioned earlier that we're expanding into next month. The brokers sent over the final paperwork, and everyone on my legal team—guys with very expensive degrees, mind you—had already signed off on it. They said it was good to go, standard boilerplate. But I always, always read through the fine print myself. I don't just blindly sign things. 

So I'm sitting there at my desk, it's maybe 7:30 PM, the office is completely empty, and I'm going line by line through this PDF. And right there on page 47, buried in this massive block of legalese about utility sub-metering, I notice they slipped in a clause that would have made us liable for the previous tenant's outstanding HVAC maintenance fees. It was worded so vaguely, just a tiny little sub-clause, maybe two sentences long, but I caught it. I immediately called our lead counsel—woke him up, actually, he was already in bed—and made him redraft the whole section before morning. 

If I had a hard time paying attention to details, that one little sentence would have cost us, I don't know, maybe forty or fifty grand over the next five years. So, no, I am hyper-focused on the details. I review the expense reports, I check the ad spend margins down to the cent, I even notice when the formatting is off on the weekly memos Sarah prints out for me. You just have to. If you don't manage the details, the details manage you, and I refuse to let that happen. So yeah, definitely not an issue for me. I'm probably more detail-oriented than half the accountants on my payroll, to be completely honest with you.
Do you often make careless mistakes when doing tasks or activities?

Careless mistakes? No, definitely not. I mean, I think that really ties right back into what I was just saying about the details, right? You just... you can't be careless when you're the one steering the ship. If I make a careless mistake, it’s not like, "Oh, whoops, let me just hit backspace and fix that." A careless mistake for me means a delay in payroll, or a lost client, or a blown quarter. So I am incredibly deliberate about everything I do. 

Actually, it’s funny you ask that, because I deal with carelessness from *other* people all the time, and it drives me absolutely up the wall. Like, just last week, one of our junior logistics guys—nice kid, fresh out of some expensive college, but man, he just does not double-check his work—he accidentally keyed in 5,000 units instead of 50,000 for a major promotional run we have coming up. Just dropped a zero. A completely careless, stupid mistake. And if I hadn't been reviewing the master inventory ledger on Sunday morning—because, you know, I'm always looking at the numbers, even on weekends, I just sit there with my coffee at like 6 AM before anyone else in the house is awake and comb through the spreadsheets—if I hadn't caught that, we would have launched a massive ad campaign with basically zero product to back it up. It would have been an absolute disaster. We would have had customers furious, vendors breathing down our necks... all because one guy couldn't take two seconds to proofread a purchase order.

So, because I know what’s on the line, I just don't allow myself to be careless. I have a whole system. I triple-check my emails before I hit send, especially if they're going to the board or a major buyer. I don't sign off on invoices unless I've seen the original purchase order. I think when you build a business from nothing, without the fancy diplomas and the safety nets, you learn early on that you can't afford to be sloppy. Every single task matters, whether you're sweeping the floors or signing a million-dollar check. So, yeah, no, careless mistakes aren't really a thing for me. I'm always completely dialed in to what I'm doing. I just don't let myself slip up like that.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by your surroundings?

Well, actually... yeah. That right there is exactly what made me come in to see you today. It’s frustrating because I just told you how dialed in I am with the details, and I am, I really am, but... for the past year or so? It’s like my filter is just completely broken. 

I’ll be in the middle of something important, totally intending to get it done, and the absolute smallest thing will completely derail me. Like, just a phone buzz. Not even a ring, just that little vibration on the desk. I get hundreds of emails and texts a day, I should be used to it, but lately, it just yanks my attention away. I’ll be looking at a profit and loss statement and the phone buzzes, and before I can even tell myself to ignore it, I’ve already dropped the report and picked up the phone. 

Or, you know, my office has these big glass walls. I thought it was a great idea when we designed the space—transparency, open-door policy, showing the team I'm in the trenches with them. But lately, if somebody just walks past my office... say, Sarah heading to the breakroom, or one of the junior guys walking by with a stack of mail... my eyes just track them. I stop what I'm doing and just watch them walk by. And by the time they're out of sight, I've completely lost my train of thought. 

And it’s not even just physical stuff in the room, either. It’s my own head. I’ll be trying to draft a critical email to a supplier, and suddenly I’ll have this completely random thought about my in-laws. Out of nowhere. I'll start thinking about whether my father-in-law is going to bring up politics at dinner this Sunday, or if we need to help them fix their roof, or whatever. Just totally unrelated personal stuff. And before I know it, I’m sitting there stressing about Sunday dinner instead of running my company. 

It just pulls me off what I’m doing before I can even stop it. Like I said, it’s been going on for about a year now, and it's driving me crazy because I don't have time to be getting pulled in a hundred different directions by every little shadow in the hallway or random thought that pops into my head. That's really what made me pick up the phone and make this appointment.
Do you find that your difficulty with distractions and focusing is consistent across different settings and tasks?

Consistent across different settings? I mean... I'm honestly not really sure. I haven't exactly noticed it happening everywhere, but to be fair, you have to understand my schedule. My entire life basically *is* the office, or a warehouse, or a client dinner. I'm putting in maybe seventy, eighty hours a week, easy. So work is really my main setting. That's where the stakes are, and that's where I'm noticing the wheels falling off, so to speak. 

When I'm actually off the clock—which is rare, my wife Claire will absolutely vouch for that, she's always getting on my case about bringing my phone to the dinner table or answering emails in bed—but when I'm actually just doing normal stuff? I don't really feel that same level of distraction. Like, if I'm out in the garage on a Sunday afternoon... I've got this '68 Mustang I've been restoring. Bought it as an absolute junker three years ago, completely rusted out, and I've been stripping it down to the frame and rebuilding it myself. When I'm out there, swapping out a carburetor or working on the suspension, I'm fine. I don't feel distracted at all. 

But then again, I'm also not trying to read a fifty-page commercial lease agreement out there, you know? It's hands-on. It's physical. If the dog barks or my neighbor walks by the driveway, yeah, I might look up, but it doesn't completely ruin my workflow the way it does when I'm sitting at my desk trying to run a quarterly profit projection. I can just go right back to turning the wrench. 

And Claire, well, she does say I don't listen to her sometimes. Like she'll be telling me this long story about her sister's kids or some drama with the neighborhood HOA, and I'll totally zone out and start thinking about supply chain logistics. But is that a clinical distraction issue, or is that just... you know, me being a husband who doesn't really care about the HOA? I really don't know. 

So I couldn't tell you for sure if it's consistent across the board. I just know I really only notice it being a massive problem when I'm trying to do the heavy mental lifting at the office. The deep work. That's where the buzzing phones and the people walking past the glass walls are just absolutely killing me. Outside of that? I haven't really paid enough attention to tell you one way or the other.
Do you think your difficulty with focusing and distractions significantly interferes with your daily life and relationships?

Significantly? I don't know if I'd use the word "significantly" in the sense that the sky is falling. I mean, I’m still keeping up overall. The business is growing, the lights are on, the bills are paid. I'm not failing at life by any stretch. But... it is definitely starting to cost me. It's costing me trust at home, and it's definitely costing me the patience of the people I work with. 

Take the office, for example. I've always prided myself on being a hands-on boss. I like to mentor the younger guys because, like I said, I didn't have the fancy high school diploma or the college degree, so I had to learn everything the hard way, and I want to pass that on. But lately, when I sit down for a mentoring conversation, things just don't go the way they should. Just last Tuesday, I was having a one-on-one with Mark, our new regional director. Great kid, really hungry. He’s sitting across from me, pouring his heart out about how to handle this tricky vendor negotiation, and right in the middle of it, I just completely lost the thread. I started wondering if the HVAC in the building was running too loud, and then I was looking at the blinds, and by the time I tuned back in, he was staring at me waiting for advice, and I had absolutely no idea what he had just said for the last five minutes. I had to ask him to repeat himself, and I could just see the wind go right out of his sails. He looked so deflated. And it’s happening in bigger meetings, too. I'll get derailed by some random thought and take the whole agenda off track, and I can literally see my executive team exchanging these tired looks. I'm wearing out their patience. 

And then at home... man, it's costing me trust with Claire. It really is. It’s not just her thinking I'm ignoring her stories about the HOA, it's when actual family plans get messed up. We had her parents' 50th anniversary dinner a couple weeks ago. Huge deal. Catered, extended family flying in, the whole nine yards. We had a strict schedule for the afternoon, and I was supposed to pick up the cake and be home by three. Well, I went to get the cake, got a ping on my phone about a shipping delay, pulled over to look at it, went down this massive rabbit hole trying to reroute freight trucks, and completely lost track of time.
